query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Face-centered cubic (FCC) metals with low Peierls stress, such as copper, can exhibit high ductility due to the ease of dislocation glide and cross-slip at standard temperature and pressure.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline copper with an average grain size of 10 micrometers
generation.intervention: Uniaxial tensile loading with a strain rate of 0.001 per second
generation.mechanism: Dislocation glide and cross-slip facilitated by the low Peierls stress in the FCC crystal structure
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in ductility, measured as a 20% increase in elongation to failure compared to a baseline of 30% for a similar FCC metal with higher Peierls stress, such as nickel
generation.baseline: Elongation to failure of 30% for nickel
generation.boundary: A minimum of 15% increase in elongation to failure to confirm the hypothesis
generation.uncertainty: The actual ductility may vary depending on the specific microstructure and impurity content of the copper sample, as well as the accuracy of the molecular dynamics simulation

falsification_experiment.design: Uniaxial tensile testing of polycrystalline copper and nickel samples with varying grain sizes and microstructures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured elongation to failure of copper is less than 40% and not significantly higher than that of nickel, the hypothesis is falsified
